title: Machines Question 1
question: An ideal machine and a practical machine are compared while lifting the same load through the same vertical height. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both must require the same input work, regardless of friction.
The practical machine requires less input work because it is easier to operate.
The ideal machine requires less input work because it has no energy losses.
The ideal machine and practical machine must have identical efficiencies.

explanation: The ideal machine has no energy losses, so its input work equals the useful work done in raising the load. A practical machine requires additional input work to overcome friction and other losses.

title: Machines Question 2
question: A claw hammer is used to pull a nail out of wood. Consider the hammer as a lever, with the point of contact with the wood acting as the fulcrum. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is a first-class lever because the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load.
It is a second-class lever because the nail lies between the effort and the fulcrum.
It is a third-class lever because the effort lies between the fulcrum and the nail.
It is always a third-class lever, irrespective of how it is used.

explanation: In the usual nail-pulling arrangement, the contact point with the wood acts as the fulcrum, between the applied effort and the nail being pulled. The hammer therefore functions as a first-class lever.

title: Machines Question 3
question: A single movable pulley is used to raise a load. The load moves upward by 20 cm while the free end of the rope is pulled downward. Assume an ideal pulley and an inextensible rope. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The effort moves downward by 10 cm, and the ideal MA is 2.
The effort moves downward by 40 cm, and the ideal MA is 2.
The effort moves downward by 40 cm, and the ideal MA is 1.
The effort moves downward by 20 cm, and the ideal MA is 2.

explanation: The movable pulley is supported by two rope segments. The effort moves twice the distance of the load, and the ideal mechanical advantage is 2.

title: Machines Question 4
question: A machine has a velocity ratio of 4 and an efficiency of 75%. A student claims that the machine's mechanical advantage is 4 because the load is supported by four sections of rope. What is the correct evaluation?

options.text: The claim is correct because the number of supporting strands always equals actual MA.
The claim is correct only when the effort acts vertically.
The actual mechanical advantage is 3; the supporting strands determine the ideal velocity ratio, not necessarily the actual MA.

explanation:
MA=(eta / 100)× VR=0.75×4=3


The actual MA is reduced by the machine's energy losses.

title: Machines Question 5
question: A uniform rod is balanced horizontally on a pivot located to the right of its centre. The rod's own weight acts downward through its centre of gravity. Which moment does the rod's weight produce about the pivot?

options.text: The direction cannot be determined even if the centre of gravity and pivot positions are known.

explanation: The rod's centre of gravity lies to the left of the pivot. A downward force acting to the left of the pivot produces an anticlockwise moment.

title: Machines Question 6
question: A first-class lever is initially in equilibrium. The effort and load remain unchanged, but the fulcrum is shifted towards the load. Assume the lever's own weight is negligible and the new arrangement is mechanically possible. What happens to the moment balance?

options.text: The effort moment increases relative to the load moment, so the lever tends to rotate unless equilibrium is restored.
Both moments must remain unchanged because the forces have not changed.
The load moment necessarily becomes zero.
The lever must remain balanced because it is still a first-class lever.

explanation: Shifting the fulcrum changes the perpendicular distances of both forces from the pivot. The moments therefore change even though the force magnitudes remain the same.

title: Machines Question 7
question: A block-and-tackle system has four supporting strands. Its efficiency is 60%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its actual MA is 4, because the number of supporting strands determines both MA and VR.
Its actual MA is 2.4, and its input work is greater than its useful output work.
Its actual MA is 1.6, and its output work is greater than its input work.

explanation:
MA=(60 / 100)×4=2.4


Because the efficiency is below 100%, some input work is lost, so the input work exceeds the useful output work.

title: Machines Question 8
question: A lever has an effort arm of 80 cm and a load arm of 20 cm. The actual mechanical advantage is 3. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Its velocity ratio is 3 and its efficiency is 100%.
Its velocity ratio is 4 and its efficiency is 75%.
Its velocity ratio is 4 and its efficiency is 133.3%.
Its velocity ratio is 0.25 and its efficiency is 75%.

explanation:
For an ideal geometrical lever arrangement,


VR=(80 / 20)=4


Therefore,


eta=(3 / 4)×100%=75%


The actual MA is lower than the VR because the lever is not perfectly efficient.

title: Machines Question 9
question: A machine is used to raise a load slowly. Its velocity ratio remains unchanged, but lubrication reduces friction. Which combination of changes is expected?
explanation: Lubrication reduces energy losses. With VR unchanged, the efficiency and actual mechanical advantage both increase because MA=(eta/100)× VR.

title: Machines Question 10
question: A student states that a machine with an efficiency of 80% loses 20% of the input work as heat or other non-useful energy. Which condition is necessary for this statement to be valid?

options.text: The machine must have a mechanical advantage of 1.
The machine must be a fixed pulley.
The efficiency must be defined as useful output work divided by input work.

explanation: Efficiency is the ratio of useful output work to input work. If efficiency is 80%, then 20% of the input work does not appear as useful output work.

title: Machines Question 11
question: An ideal machine has a mechanical advantage of 0.5. Which statement must be true?

options.text: The machine is incapable of lifting any load.
The effort moves through half the distance moved by the load.
The machine has an efficiency of 50%.
The effort is twice the load, and the effort moves through half the distance moved by the load.

explanation: For an ideal machine, MA=VR=0.5. Thus the effort is twice the load, while the effort displacement is half the load displacement. The machine is a force reducer but may provide a speed or distance advantage.

title: Machines Question 12
question: A second-class lever is used to lift a load. The load is moved closer to the fulcrum without changing the effort point. Assume the effort and load positions remain on the same side of the fulcrum. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The ideal mechanical advantage increases because the load arm decreases while the effort arm stays fixed.
The ideal mechanical advantage decreases because the load arm decreases.
The ideal mechanical advantage remains unchanged because the lever class is unchanged.
The ideal mechanical advantage becomes zero because the load is closer to the fulcrum.

explanation: For an ideal lever, MA=VR=effort arm/load arm. Decreasing the load arm while retaining the effort arm increases the ratio.

title: Machines Question 13
question: Two levers are made from identical material and have equal lengths. Lever P has a fulcrum at its centre; Lever Q has a fulcrum closer to the load. Their own weights are negligible. Which statement is necessarily correct?

options.text: P must have the greater ideal MA because its fulcrum is central.
Q can have a greater ideal MA because its effort arm is longer relative to its load arm.
Both levers must have equal ideal MA because their lengths are equal.
The ideal MA depends only on the material and length of the lever.

explanation: Mechanical advantage depends on the ratio of the effort arm to the load arm, not simply on total length or material. Moving the fulcrum towards the load can increase this ratio.

title: Machines Question 14
question: A pulley system is arranged so that the effort is applied downward while the load rises upward. Which statement correctly distinguishes the purpose of the fixed pulleys from that of the movable pulleys in a conventional block-and-tackle system?

options.text: Fixed pulleys always double the load, while movable pulleys only change direction.
Both types of pulleys always provide the same force advantage.
Fixed pulleys can redirect the effort, while the movable block and its supporting strands provide the main ideal force advantage.
Fixed pulleys eliminate friction, while movable pulleys eliminate the need for effort.

explanation: In a conventional block-and-tackle system, fixed pulleys mainly redirect the rope and make the effort more convenient. The movable block is supported by multiple rope segments, reducing the required ideal effort.

title: Machines Question 15
question: A machine has a velocity ratio of 6. Its efficiency is increased from 50% to 75% without changing the velocity ratio. What happens to its mechanical advantage?
explanation:
Initially, MA=0.50×6=3.

After the improvement, MA=0.75×6=4.5.

title: Machines Question 16
question: A load is raised through a vertical height using an inclined plane. The same load is then raised through the same height using a longer inclined plane. Both planes are assumed ideal. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The longer plane requires less effort, but the useful output work is the same.
The longer plane requires the same effort because the load is unchanged.
The longer plane requires more effort because the effort travels farther.
The longer plane performs less useful output work because it is longer.

explanation: The useful work in both cases is the same gain in gravitational potential energy, mgh. A longer ideal plane reduces the required effort by increasing the distance over which it acts.

title: Machines Question 17
question: A student argues: “Because a movable pulley has two supporting strands, the effort is always half the load.” Which correction is most accurate?

options.text: The statement is true for all movable pulleys, regardless of friction or pulley weight.
The statement is true only when the load is stationary.
The statement is false because a movable pulley always has MA less than 1.
The statement is valid for an ideal single movable pulley with a negligible pulley weight; real conditions can change the actual effort required.

explanation: In an ideal single movable pulley, the two supporting rope segments share the load equally. Friction and the weight of the movable block can increase the actual effort required.

title: Machines Question 18
question: A machine has MA=VR. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The machine must be a lever.
The machine must have a velocity ratio of 1.
The machine has 100% efficiency under the standard definitions.
The machine must have no moving parts.

explanation:
eta=(MA / VR)×100%=100%


Equality of MA and VR indicates ideal efficiency under the standard definitions.

title: Machines Question 19
question: A force acts vertically downward on a horizontal lever at a point 30 cm from the fulcrum. The force is then shifted to a point 60 cm from the fulcrum without changing its magnitude or direction. What happens to the moment magnitude?

options.text: It becomes four times as large.

explanation: The moment magnitude equals force multiplied by perpendicular distance from the pivot. Doubling the distance while keeping the force unchanged doubles the moment.

title: Machines Question 20
question: A machine raises a load with an efficiency of 40%. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its input work is 40% of its output work.
Its output work is 60% of its input work.
Its output work is 2.5 times its input work.
Its useful output work is 40% of its input work.

explanation: Efficiency is useful output work divided by input work. At 40% efficiency, the useful output work is 0.40 times the input work.

title: Machines Question 21
question: A lever is in equilibrium under a load and an effort. The load is doubled, and the effort is also doubled. The positions of both forces and the fulcrum remain unchanged. The lever was initially in equilibrium, and its own weight is negligible. What happens?

options.text: It remains in equilibrium because both opposing moments double.
It rotates towards the load because the load is doubled.
It rotates towards the effort because the effort is doubled.
It can remain in equilibrium only if the fulcrum is moved.

explanation: The initial clockwise and anticlockwise moments were equal. Doubling both forces doubles both moments by the same factor, preserving equilibrium.

title: Machines Question 22
question: An ideal block-and-tackle system has a velocity ratio of 5. The effort is applied downward, and the load rises by 12 cm. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The effort moves downward by 12 cm, and the load moves with five times the effort.
The effort moves downward by 60 cm, and the ideal MA is 5.
The effort moves downward by 60 cm, and the ideal MA is 1.
The effort moves downward by 2.4 cm, and the ideal MA is 5.

explanation: The velocity ratio is the effort displacement divided by the load displacement. Thus effort displacement =5×12=60 cm. For an ideal machine, MA=VR=5.

title: Machines Question 23
question: A real machine has a velocity ratio of 4 and an actual mechanical advantage of 2. Which statement correctly describes it?

options.text: It is ideal because the actual MA is an integer.
Its efficiency is 50%, meaning half of the input work appears as useful output work.
Its efficiency is 25%, meaning three-quarters of the input work appears as useful output work.

explanation:
eta=(MA / VR)×100%
=(2 / 4)×100%=50%


Therefore, half the input work is converted into useful output work.

title: Machines Question 24
question: A uniform rod is balanced on a fulcrum at its midpoint. A downward force is applied at one end. What must be true if the rod is to remain in rotational equilibrium?

options.text: The applied force must be zero in every possible arrangement.
The rod's weight must act at one end.
The fulcrum must be shifted to the end where the force is applied.
The net moment about the fulcrum must be zero, requiring an opposing moment from another force or support arrangement.

explanation: A single non-zero force applied away from the fulcrum produces a moment. For rotational equilibrium, an equal and opposite moment must balance it.

title: Machines Question 25
question: Which statement correctly compares a first-class lever and a second-class lever?

options.text: Both must have a mechanical advantage greater than 1.
A first-class lever may have MA greater than, equal to or less than 1 depending on the arm lengths; a second-class lever generally has ideal MA greater than 1.
A second-class lever always has MA equal to 1.
A first-class lever can never change the direction of force.

explanation: In a first-class lever, the fulcrum lies between effort and load, so the relative arm lengths can vary. In a second-class lever, the effort arm is longer than the load arm, giving an ideal MA greater than 1.

title: Machines Question 26
question: A machine's efficiency increases while the load and the distances moved by the effort and load remain unchanged. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The effort required decreases, because the useful output work remains fixed while the required input work falls.
The effort required increases because the machine has become more efficient.
The useful output work must decrease.

explanation: The load and its displacement are unchanged, so the useful output work remains fixed. Greater efficiency means less input work is required; with the effort displacement unchanged, the required effort decreases.

title: Machines Question 27
question: A pulley system contains several pulleys, but the rope is arranged so that only three rope segments support the movable block. Under ideal conditions, which statement is correct?

options.text: Its velocity ratio must equal the total number of pulleys.
Its velocity ratio must equal twice the number of movable pulleys.
Its velocity ratio is 3, regardless of how many additional pulleys merely redirect the rope.
Its velocity ratio is always 1 because the rope is continuous.

explanation: For the standard block-and-tackle arrangement, the ideal velocity ratio is determined by the number of supporting rope segments. Pulleys used only to redirect the effort do not necessarily increase that ratio.

title: Machines Question 28
question: A student says: “A machine with a high velocity ratio must have a high mechanical advantage.” Which response is scientifically correct?

options.text: Correct, because MA=VR for every real machine.
Correct, because friction increases both MA and VR equally.
Incorrect only for levers; it is always correct for pulleys.
Incorrect, because actual MA also depends on efficiency; a machine can have a high VR but a relatively low MA.

explanation: The relationship is MA=(eta/100)× VR. A high VR does not guarantee a high MA if efficiency is low.

title: Machines Question 29
question: An ideal lever raises a load by moving it through 5 cm while the effort point moves through 25 cm. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its VR is 0.2 and its ideal MA is 0.2.
Its VR is 5 and its ideal MA is 5.
Its VR is 25 and its ideal MA is 5.
Its VR is 5 and its ideal MA is 1.

explanation:
VR=(25 / 5)=5


For an ideal lever, MA=VR=5.

title: Machines Question 30
question: A student compares two machines lifting identical loads through equal vertical heights. Machine P has an efficiency of 90%, while Machine Q has an efficiency of 60%. Assume both machines operate under the standard definitions of efficiency. Which conclusion must be true?

options.text: Machine P performs more useful output work than Machine Q.
Machine Q requires less input work because it is less efficient.
Both machines must have the same input work because the loads and heights are equal.
Machine P requires less input work to perform the same useful task.

explanation: Both machines deliver the same useful output work because the loads and vertical heights are equal. Since P is more efficient, it needs less input work to deliver that same output.

title: A machine has a mechanical advantage greater than 1 but an efficiency less than 100%. Which statement must be correct?
question: A machine has a mechanical advantage greater than 1 but an efficiency less than 100%. Which statement must be correct?

options.text: The load moves faster than the effort in every case.
The effort moves through a smaller distance than the load.
The load is greater than the effort, but the effort moves through a greater distance than the load.
The machine produces more useful work than the work supplied.

explanation: A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the load exceeds the effort. Since efficiency is below 100%, input work exceeds useful output work; therefore, the effort moves through a greater distance than the load.

title: Which statement correctly distinguishes the mechanical advantage of an ideal machine from that of a real machine?
question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the mechanical advantage of an ideal machine from that of a real machine?

options.text: The mechanical advantage of an ideal machine must always be less than 1.
The mechanical advantage of an ideal machine equals its velocity ratio; for a real machine, it is generally smaller than its velocity ratio.
The mechanical advantage of a real machine is always equal to its velocity ratio.
The mechanical advantage of an ideal machine is always greater than its velocity ratio.

explanation: An ideal machine has 100% efficiency, so MA=VR. In a real machine, energy losses make efficiency less than 100%, so MA<VR.

title: A second-class lever is commonly capable of acting as a force multiplier. Which arrangement makes this possible?
question: A second-class lever is commonly capable of acting as a force multiplier. Which arrangement makes this possible?

options.text: The fulcrum lies between the effort and the load.
The effort lies between the fulcrum and the load.
The effort arm is always shorter than the load arm.
The load lies between the fulcrum and the effort.

explanation: In a second-class lever, the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort. Consequently, the effort arm is longer than the load arm, allowing a mechanical advantage greater than 1 for an ideal lever.

title: Which statement about a third-class lever is correct?
question: Which statement about a third-class lever is correct?

options.text: It has the effort between the fulcrum and the load and generally provides a speed or distance advantage rather than a force advantage.
It always has a mechanical advantage greater than 1.
It has the load between the fulcrum and the effort.
It cannot change the direction of the applied force.

explanation: In a third-class lever, the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load. The effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so its ideal mechanical advantage is less than 1, but the load can move through a greater distance.

title: A uniform metre rule is balanced horizontally on a knife edge at its centre. Equal weights are suspended at equal distances on opposite sides. One weight is then moved closer to the knife edge. What must happen if the rule is to remain balanced?
question: A uniform metre rule is balanced horizontally on a knife edge at its centre. Equal weights are suspended at equal distances on opposite sides. One weight is then moved closer to the knife edge. What must happen if the rule is to remain balanced?

options.text: The other weight must also be moved closer by the same distance.
The other weight must be moved farther from the knife edge, or its magnitude must be increased appropriately.
The knife edge must be moved towards the weight that was shifted.
No adjustment is needed because the weights are equal.

explanation: The clockwise and anticlockwise moments must remain equal. Moving one weight closer reduces its moment, so the opposing moment must also be adjusted by increasing its distance or the weight producing it.

title: A uniform lever is in equilibrium under several forces. Which statement about the principle of moments is correct?
question: A uniform lever is in equilibrium under several forces. Which statement about the principle of moments is correct?

options.text: The sum of all upward forces must equal the sum of all downward forces, regardless of their positions.
The total clockwise moment must always be greater than the total anticlockwise moment.
The algebraic sum of moments about any chosen point is zero for rotational equilibrium.
Only the moments of forces acting perpendicular to the lever need to be considered, even when other forces have perpendicular components.

explanation: For rotational equilibrium, the algebraic sum of moments about any point is zero. Forces must be considered through their perpendicular distances from the chosen pivot.

title: A single fixed pulley is used to raise a load. Why can it still be useful even when its ideal mechanical advantage is 1?
question: A single fixed pulley is used to raise a load. Why can it still be useful even when its ideal mechanical advantage is 1?

options.text: It reduces the work required to lift the load.
It doubles the force applied by the user.
It allows the load to rise farther than the rope is pulled.
It changes the direction of the applied effort, making it more convenient to pull downward.

explanation: An ideal single fixed pulley changes the direction of force without multiplying it. Pulling downward may be more convenient because the user can use body weight and a natural pulling position.

title: In an ideal single movable pulley, the load is supported by two segments of the same rope. Which conclusion follows?
question: In an ideal single movable pulley, the load is supported by two segments of the same rope. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: The effort is half the load, and the effort moves twice the distance moved by the load.
The effort equals the load, and both move through equal distances.
The effort is twice the load, and the load moves twice the effort distance.
The effort is half the load, and both move through equal distances.

explanation: The two supporting rope segments share the load equally in an ideal system. The effort is half the load, while the effort must move twice as far as the load to conserve work.

title: In a block-and-tackle arrangement, the ideal velocity ratio is determined by the number of supporting rope segments. Which statement is correct?
question: In a block-and-tackle arrangement, the ideal velocity ratio is determined by the number of supporting rope segments. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only the number of movable pulleys determines the velocity ratio in every arrangement.
The number of pulleys in the fixed block alone determines the velocity ratio.
The number of rope segments supporting the movable block determines the ideal velocity ratio.
The velocity ratio is always twice the total number of pulleys.

explanation: In the standard block-and-tackle arrangement, the ideal velocity ratio equals the number of rope segments supporting the movable block. Counting the pulleys alone can give the wrong result.

title: A pulley system has an actual mechanical advantage smaller than its velocity ratio. Which explanation is the most appropriate?
question: A pulley system has an actual mechanical advantage smaller than its velocity ratio. Which explanation is the most appropriate?

options.text: The load necessarily moves farther than the effort.
Some input energy is dissipated through effects such as friction, so not all input work becomes useful output work.
The load gains more energy than the effort supplies.
The system must contain a third-class lever.

explanation:
is the most appropriate?

A) The load necessarily moves farther than the effort.
B) Some input energy is dissipated through effects such as friction, so not all input work becomes useful output work.
C) The load gains more energy than the effort supplies.
D) The system must contain a third-class lever.

**Correct Answer: B**

**Reason:** In a real machine, friction and other losses reduce useful output work. Hence efficiency is below 100%, making MA<VR.

title: Which statement about the efficiency of a real machine is correct?
question: Which statement about the efficiency of a real machine is correct?

options.text: Efficiency is always equal to mechanical advantage.
Efficiency can exceed 100% if the load is raised slowly.
Efficiency is independent of friction and other energy losses.
Efficiency is the ratio of useful output work to input work, expressed as a percentage.

explanation:
Efficiency measures how much of the supplied work becomes useful output work:


eta=(Useful output work / Input work)×100%


It cannot exceed 100% for an ordinary passive machine.

title: A machine is lubricated, and its efficiency increases while its velocity ratio remains unchanged. Which statement follows?
question: A machine is lubricated, and its efficiency increases while its velocity ratio remains unchanged. Which statement follows?

options.text: Its input work must become zero.

explanation: Since eta=(MA/VR)×100%, increasing efficiency while keeping the velocity ratio constant means the mechanical advantage increases.

title: A lever is balanced by a load and an effort. The weight of the lever itself is neglected. If both the load and effort are doubled while their positions remain unchanged, what happens?
question: A lever is balanced by a load and an effort. The weight of the lever itself is neglected. If both the load and effort are doubled while their positions remain unchanged, what happens?

options.text: The lever remains in rotational equilibrium.
The lever balances only if the fulcrum is shifted.

explanation: Both the clockwise and anticlockwise moments double. Their equality is preserved, so the lever remains balanced.

title: A uniform lever has its fulcrum away from its centre. Why must its own weight be included when applying the principle of moments?
question: A uniform lever has its fulcrum away from its centre. Why must its own weight be included when applying the principle of moments?

options.text: Its weight always acts through the fulcrum.
Its weight acts at its centre of gravity and may produce a moment about the fulcrum.
Its weight acts at the end nearest the effort.
Its weight contributes to moments only when the lever is vertical.

explanation: The weight of a uniform lever acts at its midpoint. If the fulcrum does not pass through that point, the lever's weight generally produces a moment that must be included.

title: A machine has a velocity ratio of 5. Which statement is necessarily true under the standard definition of velocity ratio?
question: A machine has a velocity ratio of 5. Which statement is necessarily true under the standard definition of velocity ratio?

options.text: The load is five times the effort.
The machine must have five pulleys.
The effort moves five times the distance moved by the load.

explanation: Velocity ratio is the distance moved by the effort divided by the distance moved by the load. It does not, by itself, specify the force ratio, efficiency or number of pulleys.

title: Which statement about an inclined plane is correct?
question: Which statement about an inclined plane is correct?

options.text: Its ideal velocity ratio is the length of the plane divided by its vertical height.
Its ideal velocity ratio is the vertical height divided by the length of the plane.
Its ideal velocity ratio is always 1.
Its velocity ratio depends only on the mass of the load.

explanation:
For an inclined plane,


VR=(Length of plane / Vertical height)


A longer plane for the same height gives a greater ideal velocity ratio.

title: A load is raised to the same vertical height using two inclined planes. Plane X is longer than Plane Y. Assuming ideal conditions, which statement is correct?
question: A load is raised to the same vertical height using two inclined planes. Plane X is longer than Plane Y. Assuming ideal conditions, which statement is correct?

options.text: Plane X requires more effort because its length is greater.
Both planes require equal effort because the vertical height is the same.
Plane X requires less effort because its greater velocity ratio gives a smaller ideal effort for the same load.
Plane Y has the greater velocity ratio because it is shorter.

explanation: The ideal effort is E=L/VR. Since Plane X has the greater length-to-height ratio, it has the greater velocity ratio and requires less effort for the same load.

title: Why does friction reduce the efficiency of an inclined plane?
question: Why does friction reduce the efficiency of an inclined plane?

options.text: It increases the vertical height through which the load is raised.
Some input work is spent overcoming friction instead of contributing to the useful gain in gravitational potential energy.
It makes the load's weight disappear during motion.
It always increases the velocity ratio.

explanation: The useful output work is the gain in gravitational potential energy. Work done against friction is dissipated, so the useful output is smaller than the input.

title: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between mechanical advantage and velocity ratio in a real machine?
question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between mechanical advantage and velocity ratio in a real machine?

options.text: Mechanical advantage must always exceed velocity ratio.
Mechanical advantage equals velocity ratio only when the effort is applied vertically.
Mechanical advantage and velocity ratio are unrelated quantities.
Mechanical advantage is generally less than velocity ratio when the machine's efficiency is below 100%.

explanation: Since eta=(MA/VR)×100%, an efficiency below 100% implies MA<VR.

title: A machine is described as a force multiplier. Which interpretation is scientifically correct?
question: A machine is described as a force multiplier. Which interpretation is scientifically correct?

options.text: It can produce a load greater than the effort, but this does not imply that output work exceeds input work.
It creates additional energy whenever the load is raised.
It always increases both force and speed in the same proportion.

explanation: A force multiplier can increase the force exerted on the load, but this is accompanied by a corresponding distance trade-off and possibly energy losses. It cannot create energy.

title: Two machines have the same velocity ratio. Machine P has a greater efficiency than Machine Q. Which statement must be true?
question: Two machines have the same velocity ratio. Machine P has a greater efficiency than Machine Q. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Machine P necessarily has a smaller mechanical advantage.
Machine P necessarily moves the load through a greater distance.
Machine P has a greater mechanical advantage than Machine Q.
Machine P must be an ideal machine.

explanation: For each machine, MA=eta× VR, with efficiency expressed as a fraction. For the same velocity ratio, the machine with greater efficiency has greater mechanical advantage.

title: A lever is in equilibrium. A downward force is applied exactly at the fulcrum. Assuming the fulcrum provides the required support reaction, what is the direct effect of this additional force on the moment balance about the fulcrum?
question: A lever is in equilibrium. A downward force is applied exactly at the fulcrum. Assuming the fulcrum provides the required support reaction, what is the direct effect of this additional force on the moment balance about the fulcrum?

options.text: It produces zero moment about the fulcrum.

explanation: The perpendicular distance of the force's line of action from the fulcrum is zero. Therefore, its moment about the fulcrum is zero, although the support reaction may change.

title: Which statement about the work done by an ideal machine is correct?
question: Which statement about the work done by an ideal machine is correct?

options.text: Useful output work is greater than input work.
Useful output work equals input work.
Input work is always greater than useful output work.
The machine performs useful work without receiving energy.

explanation: An ideal machine has no energy losses. Therefore, input work equals useful output work and its efficiency is 100%.

title: A person uses a lever to lift a heavy load. The fulcrum is shifted closer to the load while the effort position remains fixed. Which change occurs in the ideal mechanical advantage?
question: A person uses a lever to lift a heavy load. The fulcrum is shifted closer to the load while the effort position remains fixed. Which change occurs in the ideal mechanical advantage?

options.text: It increases because the effort arm becomes longer relative to the load arm.
It decreases because the load arm becomes shorter.
It remains unchanged because the load is the same.
It becomes zero because the fulcrum has moved.

explanation: For an ideal lever, MA=VR=effort arm/load arm. Shifting the fulcrum towards the load increases the effort arm and decreases the load arm, so the ratio increases.

title: Which statement about the classification of levers is correct?
question: Which statement about the classification of levers is correct?

options.text: A lever is first-class only when the effort and load are equal.
A lever is second-class only when its mechanical advantage is exactly 2.
The class of a lever is determined by the relative positions of the fulcrum, effort and load.
The class of a lever is determined solely by the material from which it is made.

explanation: Lever classification depends on which of the three—fulcrum, effort or load—lies between the other two. The class is not determined by the magnitude of the forces or the lever's material.

title: Consider the following statements about a single fixed pulley:
question: I. It can change the direction of the applied effort. II. Its ideal mechanical advantage is 1. III. It necessarily reduces the effort to half the load. IV. Its ideal velocity ratio is 1. Which combination is correct?
explanation: An ideal single fixed pulley has MA=VR=1 and changes the direction of effort. It does not halve the effort; that force advantage is associated with an ideal single movable pulley.

title: Which statement best explains why a machine may have a mechanical advantage less than 1 yet still be useful?
question: Which statement best explains why a machine may have a mechanical advantage less than 1 yet still be useful?

options.text: It must be producing energy at a rate greater than the input power.
It may provide a speed or distance advantage, allowing the load to move farther or faster than the effort point for the relevant motion.
It must be a machine with 100% efficiency.
It must be incapable of doing useful work.

explanation: A third-class lever, for example, sacrifices force advantage to provide a greater distance and often greater speed of movement at the load. A low mechanical advantage does not mean a machine is useless.

title: A student claims: “If the velocity ratio of a machine increases, its efficiency must also increase.” Which evaluation is correct?
question: A student claims: “If the velocity ratio of a machine increases, its efficiency must also increase.” Which evaluation is correct?

options.text: The claim is always correct because efficiency equals velocity ratio.
The claim is correct only for pulleys.
The claim is incorrect because efficiency depends on the relationship between mechanical advantage and velocity ratio, not on velocity ratio alone.
The claim is always incorrect because increasing velocity ratio reduces efficiency to zero.

explanation: Efficiency is eta=(MA/VR)×100%. An increase in velocity ratio alone does not determine how the mechanical advantage changes, so efficiency may increase, decrease or remain unchanged.

title: Which statement about the principle of conservation of energy in machines is correct?
question: Which statement about the principle of conservation of energy in machines is correct?

options.text: A machine may exchange force for distance, but it cannot deliver more total energy than it receives.
A machine with a high mechanical advantage violates conservation of energy.
A machine can create energy if it operates at a low speed.
Friction increases useful output energy beyond the input energy.

explanation: Machines can change the magnitude and direction of forces, as well as the distances through which forces act. They cannot create energy; real machines dissipate some input energy.

title: Two students make the following statements about an ordinary real machine:
question: - Student P: “Its efficiency can be 100% if the effort is applied very slowly.” - Student Q: “Its efficiency may be improved by reducing friction, even if its velocity ratio remains unchanged.” Which statement is correct?

options.text: Both P and Q are correct.
P is correct, but Q is incorrect.
P is incorrect, but Q is correct.
Both P and Q are incorrect.

explanation: Applying effort slowly does not eliminate friction or other energy losses, so it does not guarantee 100% efficiency. Reducing friction can increase efficiency while the velocity ratio remains unchanged.

title: Movable pulley: Finding the pulley’s own weight
question: A movable pulley supports a load of 280,N. The upward effort is 170,N, and the system moves at constant speed. Assuming two supporting rope segments, what is the weight of the movable pulley?
explanation:
The total supported weight equals the combined tension in the two strands:


W_{total}=2E=2(170)=340,N


Therefore,


W_p=340-280=60,N


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

title: Inclined plane: Finding the height from efficiency
question: A machine in the form of an inclined plane has a length of 8,m, a mechanical advantage of 3, and an efficiency of 75%. What is the vertical height of the plane?
explanation:
eta=(MA / VR)×100



75=(3 / VR)×100



VR=4


For an inclined plane,


VR=(l / h)


Thus,


h=(8 / 4)=2,m


Option D results from incorrectly using the mechanical advantage as the velocity ratio.

title: Energy conservation: Finding the input work
question: A machine raises a 900,N load through 2.5,m. Its efficiency is 60%. What input work is required?
explanation:
Useful output work:


W_{out}=900(2.5)=2250,J


Since


eta=frac{W_{out}}{W_{in}}



W_{in}=(2250 / 0.60)=3750,J


Therefore, input work is 3.75,kJ.

title: First-class lever: Calculating the fulcrum position
question: A weightless lever is 1.5,m long. A load of 240,N acts at the left end, and an upward effort of 80,N acts at the right end. The lever balances horizontally. How far is the fulcrum from the left end?
explanation:
Let the fulcrum be x metres from the left end. Its distance from the right end is 1.5-x.

By the principle of moments,


240x=80(1.5-x)



240x=120-80x



320x=120



x=0.375,m


Option C incorrectly assumes equal lever arms.

title: Real machine: Finding the wasted power
question: A machine takes in 600,W of power and operates at 85% efficiency. What is the power dissipated through friction, sound and heating?
explanation:
Useful output power:


P_{out}=0.85(600)=510,W


Wasted power:


P_{wasted}=600-510=90,W


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

title: Combined numerical problem: MA, VR and efficiency
question: A machine raises a load of 720,N using an effort of 180,N. During the operation, the effort moves 2.4,m while the load moves 0.6,m. Calculate its efficiency and the energy wasted if the effort completes this displacement once.
explanation:
Mechanical advantage:


MA=(720 / 180)=4


Velocity ratio:


VR=(2.4 / 0.6)=4


Therefore,


eta=frac44×100=100%


Input work:


W_{in}=180(2.4)=432,J


Useful output work:


W_{out}=720(0.6)=432,J


Thus, the energy wasted is 0,J. The correct answer is **D**, not B.

title: Compound machine: Two stages of mechanical advantage
question: A compound machine consists of two ideal stages. The first stage has a mechanical advantage of 3, and its output drives the second stage, which has a mechanical advantage of 4. If an effort of 25,N is applied to the first stage, what load can the second stage raise?
explanation:
The first stage produces an output force of


25×3=75,N


This becomes the effort on the second stage:


L=75×4=300,N


The correct answer is **C**, not D. The overall mechanical advantage is the product 3×4=12, giving 25×12=300,N.

title: Lever with bar weight and an unknown fulcrum position
question: A uniform 2.4,m bar weighs 120,N. A 300,N load acts at the left end, and a downward effort of 100,N acts at the right end. The bar balances horizontally. Find the distance of the fulcrum from the left end.
explanation:
Let the fulcrum be x metres from the left end. The bar's weight acts at its centre, 1.2,m from the left end.

For equilibrium, the upward and downward moments about the fulcrum must balance. The downward effort at the right end and the bar's weight contribute clockwise moments if the fulcrum lies left of the centre.

Using moments about the left end is not sufficient because the reaction at the fulcrum is unknown. Taking moments about the fulcrum:


300x=100(2.4-x)+120(1.2-x)



300x=240-100x+144-120x



520x=384



x≈0.738,m


The nearest listed answer is 0.8,m, but the exact value does not match. This question should be recalibrated rather than treated as an exact multiple-choice item.

title: Inclined plane: Frictional work and efficiency
question: A 400,N load is pulled up a rough inclined plane of length 5,m and height 3,m. The effort parallel to the plane is 300,N. Calculate the work done against friction.
explanation:
Input work:


W_{in}=300×5=1500,J


Useful work against gravity:


W_{useful}=400×3=1200,J


Work dissipated against friction:


W_f=1500-1200=300,J


The correct answer is **A**, not C.

title: Block and tackle with a real-machine efficiency
question: A block-and-tackle system has eight supporting strands and an efficiency of 75%. It lifts a load of 1,200,N. What effort is required?
explanation:
VR=8



MA=(75 / 100)×8=6


Hence,


E=(1200 / 6)=200,N


Option A assumes an ideal machine with 100% efficiency.

title: Power and energy loss in a machine
question: A machine raises a 600,N load through 5,m in 10,s. Its input power is 400,W. How much energy is lost during this operation?
explanation:
Useful output work:


W_{out}=600×5=3000,J


Input energy:


W_{in}=400×10=4000,J


Energy lost:


W_{lost}=4000-3000=1000,J
=1,kJ


The correct answer is **A**, not B.

title: Lever: Finding effort when the bar has its own weight
question: A uniform 1.5,m bar weighs 60,N. The fulcrum is at the centre. A load of 200,N acts 0.5,m to the left of the fulcrum, and an upward effort acts 0.75,m to the right. Find the effort required for equilibrium.
explanation:
The bar's weight acts through the fulcrum, so its moment is zero.


200(0.5)=E(0.75)



E=(100 / 0.75)=133.3,N


Option B uses an incorrect effort arm.

title: Movable pulley: Acceleration is not constant speed
question: A 180,N load is attached to an ideal movable pulley. The upward effort is 120,N. What is the net force on the movable assembly, including the load, and in which direction does it act? Ignore the pulley’s mass.
explanation:
Two rope segments each have tension 120,N, so the total upward force is


2T=240,N


The downward load is 180,N, giving a net force of


240-180=60,N


The net force is actually **60,N upward**, so the correct answer is **A**, not B. A downward net force would occur only if the total downward force exceeded the upward support.

title: Real machine: Finding the load from the energy balance
question: A machine receives 3,000,J of input work. Its efficiency is 80%. If it raises a load vertically through 4,m, what is the load?
explanation:
Useful output work:


W_{out}=0.8(3000)=2400,J


Since W_{out}=Lh,


L=(2400 / 4)=600,N


Option D incorrectly uses the input energy as useful output.

title: Lever: Effort applied at an angle
question: A weightless lever has a load of 240,N acting 25,cm from the fulcrum. An effort is applied 50,cm from the fulcrum at 30^° to the vertical. Find the effort required for equilibrium.
explanation:
The vertical component of the effort is Ecos30^°.


240(0.25)=Ecos30^°(0.50)



E=(60 / 0.50(0.866))
≈138.6,N


Option A assumes the effort acts perpendicular to the lever.

title: Inclined plane: Determining effort from frictional force
question: A 600,N load is pulled up a rough inclined plane of length 10,m and height 4,m. The frictional force is 60,N. Find the effort needed to move the load at constant speed, parallel to the plane.
explanation:
The component of the load's weight along the plane is


L(h / l)=600(4 / 10)=240,N


Friction adds another 60,N, so


E=240+60=300,N


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

title: Block and tackle: Inferring the load from effort displacement
question: An ideal block-and-tackle system has a velocity ratio of 6. The effort moves through 1.8,m, and the load rises through 0.3,m. If the applied effort is 150,N, what load is raised?
explanation:
The displacement ratio confirms


VR=(1.8 / 0.3)=6


For an ideal machine, MA=VR=6. Thus,


L=MA× E=6(150)=900,N


Option B incorrectly uses a ratio of 5.

title: Comparing two machines by efficiency
question: Machine P raises a 400,N load through 2,m using 1,200,J of input work. Machine Q raises a 500,N load through 1.5,m using 1,000,J of input work. Which statement is correct?

options.text: P is more efficient by 5 percentage points.
Q is more efficient by 5 percentage points.
P is more efficient by 10 percentage points.

explanation:
For P:


eta_P=(400(2) / 1200)×100
=66.7%


For Q:


eta_Q=(500(1.5) / 1000)×100
=75%


Thus Q is more efficient by approximately 8.3 percentage points. The correct answer is not among the options; this item is withdrawn rather than assigning a false comparison.

title: Lever: Calculating the load from mechanical advantage
question: A lever operates with an effort of 80,N. Its measured mechanical advantage is 4.5. What load does it raise?
explanation:
MA=(L / E)


Therefore,


L=MA× E=4.5(80)=360,N


Option A incorrectly uses a mechanical advantage of 4.

title: Power and velocity ratio in an ideal machine
question: An ideal machine raises a 600,N load at a speed of 0.2,m/s. Its velocity ratio is 4. What is the required input power?
explanation:
For an ideal machine, MA=VR=4, so


E=(600 / 4)=150,N


The effort speed is four times the load speed:


v_E=4(0.2)=0.8,m/s


Input power:


P=Ev_E=150(0.8)=120,W


The correct answer is **B**, not C.

title: Useful power versus input power
question: A machine lifts a 800,N load vertically through 4,m in 8,s. Its input power is 500,W. Calculate its efficiency.
explanation:
Useful work:


W_{out}=800×4=3200,J


Useful output power:


P_{out}=(3200 / 8)=400,W


Therefore,


eta=(400 / 500)×100=80%


Option C confuses useful output power with input power or rounds an incorrect intermediate value.

title: Block and tackle: Actual effort and velocity ratio
question: An ideal block-and-tackle system has five rope segments supporting its movable block. It raises a 750,N load at constant speed. What effort is required, and how far must the effort move to raise the load by 24,cm?
explanation:
For an ideal block and tackle with five supporting strands,


VR=5,qquad MA=5


Effort:


E=(750 / 5)=150,N


Effort displacement:


d_E=VR× d_L=5×24=120,cm


Option C calculates the effort correctly but uses an incorrect displacement.

title: Finding the velocity ratio from measured efficiency
question: A machine has a mechanical advantage of 3.2 and an efficiency of 64%. What is its velocity ratio?
explanation:
64=(3.2 / VR)×100


Rearranging,


VR=(3.2×100 / 64)=5


Option C assumes MA and VR are equal, which is true only for an ideal machine with 100% efficiency.

title: Lever with an inclined effort
question: A weightless lever has a load of 180,N acting 20,cm from the fulcrum. An effort acts 60,cm from the fulcrum at 30^° to the vertical. What effort is needed for equilibrium?
explanation:
The vertical component of the effort is Ecos30^°.


180(0.20)=Ecos30^°(0.60)



E=(36 / 0.60cos30^°)
≈69.3,N


The correct answer is **C**, not B. The effort must be approximately 69.3,N, because only its perpendicular component contributes to the moment.

title: Energy dissipated over repeated operations
question: A machine receives 1.5,kJ of input work per cycle and delivers 1.05,kJ of useful output work per cycle. If it performs 40 identical cycles, how much energy is wasted in total?
explanation:
Energy wasted per cycle:


W_{wasted}=1.5-1.05=0.45,kJ


For 40 cycles:


W_{total}=40×0.45=18,kJ


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

title: Inclined plane: Calculating efficiency from effort and geometry
question: A 600,N load is raised steadily along an inclined plane of length 10,m and height 4,m. The effort parallel to the plane is 300,N. Calculate the efficiency.
explanation:
VR=(10 / 4)=2.5



MA=(600 / 300)=2


Hence,


eta=(2 / 2.5)×100=80%


The correct answer is **D**, not C.

title: Finding the load using efficiency and effort
question: A real machine has a velocity ratio of 6, an efficiency of 50%, and an applied effort of 90,N. What load can it raise steadily?
explanation:
MA=(eta× VR / 100)
=(50×6 / 100)=3


Therefore,


L=MA× E=3×90=270,N


Option D incorrectly assumes the machine has ideal mechanical advantage equal to its velocity ratio.

title: Lever: Comparing the distances moved
question: A rigid lever rotates through a small angle. The effort acts 75,cm from the fulcrum and the load acts 25,cm from the fulcrum. If the load rises by 4,cm, how far does the effort point move?
explanation:
For a small angular displacement, distances moved are proportional to the distances from the fulcrum.


(d_E / d_L)=(75 / 25)=3



d_E=3×4=12,cm


Option B underestimates the displacement ratio.

title: Fixed pulley: Finding the effort from measured work
question: A real fixed pulley raises a 200,N load through 1.5,m. The effort moves through the same distance, and the total input work is 360,J. What effort is applied?
explanation:
Input work is


W_{in}=Ed_E


Therefore,


E=(360 / 1.5)=240,N


The useful output work is 200×1.5=300,J, so the efficiency is 300/360×100=83.3%. Option A incorrectly assumes no frictional losses.

title: Power required to pull a load up an inclined plane
question: A 400,N load is pulled up a rough inclined plane by a 160,N effort parallel to the surface. The load moves at a steady speed of 1.5,m/s. What is the input power?
explanation:
Input power is effort multiplied by the speed of its point of application:


P_{in}=Ev=160×1.5=240,W


Option C incorrectly uses the load rather than the effort.

title: Movable pulley with an extra downward force
question: A movable pulley supports a 280,N load. The pulley itself weighs 20,N, and an additional downward force of 40,N acts on the movable assembly. The assembly rises at constant speed. Find the effort.
explanation:
Total downward force:


W=280+20+40=340,N


Two rope segments support the assembly:


2E=340



E=170,N


The correct answer is **D**, not C.

title: Bar weight and moment balance
question: A uniform horizontal bar 1.6,m long weighs 80,N. It is supported at a fulcrum 0.4,m from its left end. A 160,N load acts at the left end. A downward effort is applied at the right end. Find the effort required for equilibrium.
explanation:
The effort arm is 1.2,m. The bar’s centre is 0.4,m to the right of the fulcrum.

The load’s anticlockwise moment is


160(0.4)=64,N,m


The bar’s clockwise moment is


80(0.4)=32,N,m


Thus,


64=32+1.2E



E=(32 / 1.2)=26.7,N


The correct effort is 26.7,N, which is absent from the options. The item is invalid as originally written and should not be scored.

title: Block and tackle: Efficiency from measured effort
question: A block-and-tackle system has six supporting strands. It raises a load of 900,N using an effort of 200,N. Calculate its efficiency.
explanation:
VR=6



MA=(900 / 200)=4.5


Therefore,


eta=(4.5 / 6)×100=75%


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

title: Energy loss and efficiency in a lifting machine
question: A machine uses 5,kJ of input energy to raise a load through a height of 2,m. If the load weighs 1,750,N, find the energy wasted.
explanation:
Useful output work:


W_{out}=1750×2=3500,J
=3.5,kJ


Energy wasted:


W_{wasted}=5-3.5=1.5,kJ


Option D gives the useful output energy rather than the wasted energy.

title: Efficiency, mechanical advantage and load
question: A machine has a velocity ratio of 4, and 25% of the input energy is lost. An effort of 125,N is applied. What load can the machine raise steadily?
explanation:
If 25% of the input energy is lost, efficiency is 75%.


MA=(75×4 / 100)=3


Therefore,


L=MA× E=3×125=375,N


Option D assumes 100% efficiency and incorrectly equates MA with VR.

title: Efficiency and effort in a real machine
question: A machine has a velocity ratio of 5 and an efficiency of 72%. It raises a load of 450,N uniformly. What effort is required?
explanation:
First calculate mechanical advantage:


eta=(MA / VR)×100



MA=(72×5 / 100)=3.6


Since MA=L/E,


E=(450 / 3.6)=125,N


Option A assumes an ideal machine, ignoring the stated efficiency.

title: A movable pulley with a non-negligible mass
question: A movable pulley of mass 6,kg supports a load of 240,N. The system rises at constant speed. Find the upward effort applied to the free end of the ideal rope.
explanation:
Pulley weight:


W_p=mg=6×10=60,N


Total supported weight:


W=240+60=300,N


Two rope segments support the movable assembly:


2E=300Rightarrow E=150,N


The correct answer is **D**, not B. Option B underestimates the effort by ignoring part of the total weight.

title: Work input, useful output and efficiency
question: A machine receives 2.4,kJ of work and raises a 600,N load vertically through 3,m. What is its efficiency?
explanation:
Useful output work:


W_{out}=600×3=1800,J


Input work:


W_{in}=2.4,kJ=2400,J


Therefore,


eta=(1800 / 2400)×100=75%


Option D results from an incorrect conversion or division.

title: Lever with a heavy bar and an off-centre fulcrum
question: A uniform 2,m bar weighs 80,N. A fulcrum is placed 0.5,m from its left end. A 200,N load is attached at the left end, and an upward effort acts at the right end. Find the effort needed for equilibrium.
explanation:
The load arm is 0.5,m; the effort arm is 1.5,m. The bar’s centre lies 0.5,m to the right of the fulcrum.

Taking moments about the fulcrum:


200(0.5)=E(1.5)+80(0.5)



100=1.5E+40



E=40,N


Option C ignores the lever arm of the bar’s own weight.

title: Inclined plane with friction
question: A 500,N load is pulled uniformly up a rough inclined plane of length 8,m and height 2,m. The applied effort parallel to the plane is 200,N. What is the frictional force?
explanation:
The component of the load’s weight down the plane is


L(h / l)=500(2 / 8)=125,N


At constant speed,


E=125+f



f=200-125=75,N


The correct answer is **B**, not C. Option C incorrectly treats the effort in excess of the gravitational component as 100,N.

question: Which pair gives the ideal efforts required on P and Q, respectively?

Wasted energy:


W_{wasted}=1200-900=300,J


Percentage wasted:


(300 / 1200)×100=25%


The correct answer is **C**, not D. The remaining energy is one-quarter of the input.

title: First-class lever with the bar’s weight acting on the opposite side
question: What effort is required for equilibrium?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 155" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 65 H315" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M122 68 L105 96 H139 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M25 15 V57" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M19 46 L25 58 L31 46" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="25" y="12" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">180 N</text><path d="M170 15 V57" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M164 46 L170 58 L176 46" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="170" y="12" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#7c3aed">60 N</text><path d="M315 112 V70" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M309 82 L315 70 L321 82" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="315" y="126" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">E</text><text x="122" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F</text><path d="M25 136 H122 M122 136 H315" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="73" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.4 m</text><text x="218" y="149" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.8 m</text></svg>
explanation:
The load produces an anticlockwise moment about F:


180(0.4)=72,N,m


The bar's centre is 0.2,m to the right of F, so its weight produces a clockwise moment of


60(0.2)=12,N,m


The effort arm is 0.8,m. Therefore,


72=12+0.8E



E=(60 / 0.8)=75,N


The correct effort is 75,N, which is absent from the choices. This question is invalid as originally offered; the correct answer must not be forced to match an incorrect option.

title: Movable pulley with an additional downward force
question: What is the effort required to raise the system at constant speed?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 195" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M35 20 H305" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M75 23 V91 A45 45 0 0 0 165 91 V43" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2.5" /><circle cx="120" cy="91" r="25" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M120 116 V127" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="82" y="127" width="76" height="30" rx="3" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><text x="120" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#111827">250 N</text><path d="M120 157 V180" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M114 169 L120 181 L126 169" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="132" y="178" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">50 N</text><path d="M165 79 V40" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M159 51 L165 39 L171 51" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="181" y="48" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">E</text></svg>
explanation:
The total downward force is


250+50=300,N


Two rope segments support the assembly, so


2E=300Rightarrow E=150,N


The correct answer is **B**, not C. Option C would result from an incorrect total-force calculation.

title: Inclined plane: Horizontal projection is not the slope length
question: What is the velocity ratio of the inclined plane?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 140 H290 L290 44 Z" fill="#cbd5e1" fill-opacity="0.45" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M30 140 L290 44" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M274 44 V140" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="4 3" /><text x="160" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">Base = 8 m</text><text x="298" y="93" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">6 m</text><text x="125" y="77" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">Slope = 10 m</text><path d="M290 140 H274 V124" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none" /></svg>
explanation:
The velocity ratio uses the sloping length divided by the vertical height:


VR=(l / h)=(10 / 6)=frac53


The horizontal base is not used in this formula. Option A uses h/l.

title: Lever experiment: Finding the missing load
question: What is the load, assuming equilibrium?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 135" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 60 H315" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M100 63 L83 91 H117 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M32 14 V52" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M26 41 L32 53 L38 41" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="32" y="12" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">L</text><path d="M315 102 V64" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M309 76 L315 64 L321 76" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="315" y="116" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">40 N</text><text x="100" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="65" y="131" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">25 cm</text><text x="207" y="131" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">75 cm</text></svg>
explanation:
Using the principle of moments:


L(25)=40(75)



L=(3000 / 25)=120,N


Option C reverses the lever-arm ratio and gives the wrong force relationship.

title: Fixed pulley: Comparing input and useful work
question: What is the efficiency of the pulley?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 130" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M35 16 H285" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><circle cx="155" cy="43" r="22" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M133 43 V87 M177 43 V87" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2.5" /><rect x="111" y="87" width="44" height="25" rx="2" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><text x="133" y="103" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#111827">150 N</text><path d="M177 60 V90" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M171 79 L177 91 L183 79" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="191" y="77" font-size="10" fill="#2563eb">Effort</text><text x="17" y="125" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Load rises 2 m; effort moves 2 m</text></svg>
explanation:
Useful output work:


W_{out}=150×2=300,J


Input work is 400,J.


eta=(300 / 400)×100=75%


The remaining 100,J is lost, mainly through friction. Option D overestimates the useful fraction.

title: Lever: A horizontal force applied at an angle
question: What effort balances the lever?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 330 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 70 H305" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M120 73 L103 100 H137 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M42 15 V62" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M36 50 L42 62 L48 50" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="42" y="12" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">120 N</text><path d="M270 70 L248 32" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M247 46 L247 31 L261 36" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="270" y="27" font-size="10" fill="#2563eb">E</text><path d="M270 70 H245" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="252" y="83" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">60°</text><text x="120" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="81" y="137" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">30 cm</text><text x="201" y="137" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">60 cm</text></svg>
explanation:
Only the vertical component of effort creates a moment about the pivot:


120(0.30)=Esin60^°(0.60)



E=(36 / 0.60(0.866))
≈69.3,N


Option B assumes the effort acts perpendicular to the lever, ignoring the stated angle.

title: Movable pulley: The pulley has mass
question: What effort is needed? Take g=10,N/kg.
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 18 H290" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M70 21 V78 A42 42 0 0 0 154 78 V43" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2.5" /><circle cx="112" cy="78" r="23" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M112 101 V112" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="76" y="112" width="72" height="29" rx="3" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><text x="112" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#111827">160 N</text><path d="M154 65 V34" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M148 45 L154 33 L160 45" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="169" y="43" font-size="10" fill="#2563eb">E</text><text x="190" y="81" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Pulley mass = 4 kg</text></svg>
explanation:
The pulley’s weight is


W_p=mg=4×10=40,N


Total supported weight:


W=160+40=200,N


Two strands support the assembly:


2E=200Rightarrow E=100,N


Option A ignores the pulley’s own weight.

title: Inclined plane: Finding friction from the measured effort
question: What is the frictional force opposing the motion?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 125 H285 L285 48 Z" fill="#cbd5e1" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M25 125 L285 48" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="134" y="80" width="36" height="23" rx="2" transform="rotate(-16.5 152 91)" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M164 78 L207 65" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M195 59 L209 64 L199 73" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="211" y="60" font-size="10" fill="#16a34a">220 N</text><text x="130" y="143" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">5 m</text><text x="291" y="91" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">3 m</text></svg>
explanation:
The component of the load’s weight parallel to the plane is


300(3 / 5)=180,N


At constant speed, the effort balances this component plus friction:


220=180+f



f=40,N


The correct answer is **A**, not B. Option B results from an incorrect subtraction.

title: Power of a machine: Distinguishing power from work
question: What is the efficiency of the machine?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M30 20 H290" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M160 24 V67" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2.5" /><rect x="124" y="67" width="72" height="37" rx="3" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><text x="160" y="89" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#111827">400 N</text><path d="M217 100 V65" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M211 77 L217 65 L223 77" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="228" y="77" font-size="10" fill="#16a34a">2.5 m</text><text x="160" y="126" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Time = 5 s</text></svg>
explanation:
Useful work:


W_{out}=400(2.5)=1000,J


Useful output power:


P_{out}=(1000 / 5)=200,W


Therefore,


eta=(200 / 250)×100=80%


Option D incorrectly assumes that all input power becomes useful output power.

title: First-class lever: Effort and load on opposite sides, with a changed pivot
question: What is the effort needed for equilibrium?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 135" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 60 H295" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M93 63 L76 91 H110 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M25 14 V52" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M19 41 L25 53 L31 41" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="25" y="12" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">240 N</text><path d="M295 100 V64" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M289 76 L295 64 L301 76" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="295" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">E</text><text x="93" y="106" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="58" y="131" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.25 m</text><text x="194" y="131" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.75 m</text></svg>
explanation:
Using the principle of moments:


240(0.25)=E(0.75)



E=(60 / 0.75)=80,N


Option A results from dividing by the full lever length rather than the actual effort arm.

title: Pulley system: Identifying the correct displacement relationship
question: How far does the free end move in the stated arrangement?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 18 H300" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><rect x="55" y="32" width="210" height="16" rx="2" fill="#cbd5e1" stroke="#64748b" /><circle cx="110" cy="95" r="23" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="210" cy="95" r="23" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><path d="M87 95 V47 M133 95 V47 M187 95 V47 M233 95 V47" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M110 118 V128 M210 118 V128" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="120" y="128" width="80" height="26" rx="3" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><text x="160" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#111827">Load</text><path d="M265 48 V80" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M259 69 L265 81 L271 69" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="277" y="73" font-size="10" fill="#2563eb">E</text></svg>
explanation:
For four supporting strands,


VR=(d_E / d_L)=4


Thus,


d_E=4(12)=48,cm


Option C would apply to a two-strand movable-pulley arrangement.

title: Inclined plane: Calculating efficiency from forces and geometry
question: What is the efficiency of the plane?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 125 H290 L290 45 Z" fill="#cbd5e1" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M25 125 L290 45" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="143" y="79" width="36" height="23" rx="2" transform="rotate(-16.8 161 90)" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M170 77 L213 64" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M201 58 L215 63 L205 72" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="218" y="61" font-size="10" fill="#16a34a">180 N</text><text x="143" y="143" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">6 m</text><text x="296" y="88" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">2 m</text></svg>
explanation:
VR=(6 / 2)=3



MA=(360 / 180)=2


Therefore,


eta=frac23×100=66.7%


The correct answer is **C**, not A. Option A would result from using an incorrect velocity ratio.

title: Lever: Finding the centre of gravity from a balancing diagram
question: What upward effort balances the bar?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 140" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 60 H300" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M160 63 L143 91 H177 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M112 13 V52" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M106 41 L112 53 L118 41" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="112" y="11" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">120 N</text><path d="M300 101 V64" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M294 76 L300 64 L306 76" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="300" y="116" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#2563eb">E</text><path d="M160 14 V52" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M154 41 L160 53 L166 41" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="160" y="11" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#7c3aed">90 N</text><text x="160" y="107" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="136" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.3 m</text><text x="235" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.9 m</text></svg>
explanation:
The bar’s own weight acts at F, so it produces zero moment about F.


120(0.3)=E(0.9)



E=(36 / 0.9)=40,N


Option C incorrectly assigns a moment to the bar’s weight even though it acts through the pivot.

title: Machine: Comparing input power and useful output power
question: What is the efficiency?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M35 18 H285" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><path d="M160 22 V57" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2.5" /><rect x="124" y="57" width="72" height="35" rx="3" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><text x="160" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#111827">500 N</text><path d="M218 93 V56" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M212 68 L218 56 L224 68" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="229" y="70" font-size="10" fill="#16a34a">3 m</text><text x="160" y="119" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Time = 10 s</text><text x="160" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Input power = 200 W</text></svg>
explanation:
Useful work:


W_{out}=500(3)=1500,J


Useful output power:


P_{out}=(1500 / 10)=150,W



eta=(150 / 200)×100=75%


The correct answer is **C**, not B.

title: Inclined plane: Determining the direction of friction
question: Which statement about friction is correct while the block moves upward?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 175" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 145 H290 L290 52 Z" fill="#cbd5e1" fill-opacity="0.5" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M25 145 L290 52" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><rect x="137" y="85" width="38" height="26" rx="2" transform="rotate(-19.3 156 98)" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M156 98 L200 83" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M188 77 L202 82 L192 91" fill="none" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="207" y="80" font-size="10" fill="#16a34a">Effort</text><path d="M149 107 L112 120" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M123 113 L110 121 L123 124" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="76" y="128" font-size="10" fill="#dc2626">Friction</text><path d="M156 98 V144" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M150 132 L156 144 L162 132" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="162" y="139" font-size="10" fill="#7c3aed">Weight</text><path d="M156 98 L141 57" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M135 69 L141 56 L148 66" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="113" y="54" font-size="10" fill="#2563eb">Normal</text></svg>

options.text: Friction acts perpendicular to the plane.
Friction acts down the plane, opposing the motion.
Friction acts vertically downward in every inclined-plane problem.

explanation:
Friction acts parallel to the contact surface and opposes the relative motion or tendency of motion. Since the block moves upward along the plane, friction acts downward along the plane.

Option D confuses friction with the vertical gravitational force.

title: Block and tackle: Determining the number of supporting strands from displacement
question: What is the velocity ratio inferred from the displacement measurements?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 320 165" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M25 18 H295" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" /><rect x="72" y="30" width="176" height="35" rx="3" fill="#cbd5e1" stroke="#64748b" /><circle cx="112" cy="47" r="13" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="160" cy="47" r="13" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="208" cy="47" r="13" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><rect x="72" y="92" width="176" height="35" rx="3" fill="#cbd5e1" stroke="#64748b" /><circle cx="112" cy="109" r="13" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="160" cy="109" r="13" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><circle cx="208" cy="109" r="13" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M99 47 V109 M125 109 V47 M147 47 V109 M173 109 V47 M195 47 V109 M221 109 V47" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" /><text x="160" y="151" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">Effort: 90 cm; load: 15 cm</text></svg>
explanation:
VR=(d_E / d_L)=(90 / 15)=6


The ratio is obtained from the actual displacement measurements, not merely from counting pulleys. Option C is a likely counting error.
