title: The Load on a Wheelbarrow
question: A load of 200 N is carried in a wheelbarrow at a distance of 0.4 m from the wheel axle (fulcrum). If the effort is applied vertically upwards at a distance of 1.2 m from the axle, what is the minimum effort required to lift the load?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 150" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="42" cy="111" r="16" fill="none" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="3" /><circle cx="42" cy="111" r="3" fill="#64748b" /><path d="M42 111 L266 51" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M266 51 L309 39" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M101 95 L140 55 L176 87 Z" fill="#cbd5e1" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="2" /><path d="M140 55 L140 24" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M134 35 L140 23 L146 35" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="140" y="18" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">L</text><path d="M289 35 V8" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M283 19 L289 7 L295 19" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="306" y="12" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">E</text><text x="42" y="139" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F</text><path d="M42 132 H140 M140 132 H289" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="91" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">40 cm</text><text x="214" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">120 cm from F</text></svg>

title: Third-class lever: Distinguishing MA from VR
question: If the lever is in equilibrium, which pair correctly gives the effort and the ideal velocity ratio?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 145" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M38 80 H307" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M38 83 L22 111 H54 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" /><path d="M78 29 V72" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M72 40 L78 28 L84 40" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="78" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2563eb">E</text><path d="M278 29 V72" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M272 62 L278 74 L284 62" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="278" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#dc2626">60 N</text><text x="38" y="125" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor">F</text><path d="M38 117 H78 M78 117 H278" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 3" /><text x="58" y="139" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9" fill="currentColor">5 cm</text><text x="178" y="139" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">30 cm from F</text></svg>
explanation:
Taking moments about the elbow:


E×5=60×30



E=(1800 / 5)=360,N


The ideal VR is the effort-arm to load-arm ratio:


VR=(5 / 30)=frac16


This means the correct physical pair is E=360,N and VR=frac16, which is **option B**.

Option D incorrectly uses the reciprocal of VR. A third-class lever can require an effort greater than its load while providing a distance or speed advantage.

question: What upward effort is needed to balance the bar?
diagramSvg: <svg class="q-diagram-svg" viewBox="0 0 340 160" width="100%" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M24 70 H316" stroke="#64748b" stroke-width="5" stroke-linecap="round" /><path d="M96 73 L79 101 H113 Z" fill="#94a3b8" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="1.5" /><path d="M24 17 V61" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M18 50 L24 62 L30 50" fill="none" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="24" y="12" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#dc2626">200 N</text><path d="M316 114 V79" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M310 90 L316 78 L322 90" fill="none" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="316" y="128" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="#2563eb">E</text><path d="M170 22 V60" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><path d="M164 49 L170 61 L176 49" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="2.5" /><text x="170" y="16" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="#7c3aed">100 N</text><text x="96" y="115" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">F</text><text x="24" y="145" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">A</text><text x="316" y="145" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">B</text><text x="58" y="137" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">0.5 m</text><text x="205" y="137" font-size="10" fill="currentColor">1.5 m</text></svg>

Take moments about F. The load at A produces an anticlockwise moment:


200×0.5=100,N,m


The bar’s weight acts at its centre, 1.0,m from A, which is 0.5,m to the right of F. It produces a clockwise moment of 100×0.5=50,N,m.

The effort acts 1.5,m from F and produces an anticlockwise moment:


E(1.5)+100=50


Thus,


E=-33.3,N


The negative result means the assumed upward effort cannot balance this configuration; the effort must act downward. Therefore, the question as drawn has no valid listed answer. **This item is withdrawn and will be replaced by a physically consistent question.
